Confirmed independently by the consumer in src/lib/colour-extract.ts lines 54-75 (garmentPixels), which treats the cutout file exactly this way: `ts const n = info.width * info.height; let clear = 0; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) if (data[4 * i + 3] < 128) clear++; const hasCutout = clear > 0.05 * n; // a real cut-out has a transparent background ... if (hasCutout ? a < 128 : bg![i]) continue; ` It calls sharp(image).ensureAlpha().raw() and uses alpha < 128 directly as "not garment". So you can derive a binary garment mask straight from the alpha channel of cutout_path (alpha ≥ 128 → garment, < 128 → background) using the same threshold this code already uses. No white/solid compositing happens anywhere in this pipeline. ## 2. Internally self.clip(imgs) batches over the list (clip(self, imgs, batch=64), lines 43-50) and np.stack([self.shape(m) for m in masks]) iterates the mask list. So for one image you must call it as ex.features([img], [mask]), and the result is a (1, 542) array — not a single 1-D vector; you'd index [0] to get the per-image feature row. Output dim: CLIP_DIM, OUT_DIM = 512, 512 + 24 + 6 → 542 total. - Extractor.__init__ (lines 24-29) loads open_clip.create_model_and_transforms("ViT-B-32", pretrained="laion2b_s34b_b79k"), picks device "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" — no CUDA branch. - Extractor.square(img) (lines 31-36) pads to a white square before CLIP preprocessing (used inside clip()), separate from the garment mask used for shape(). - mask must be an array shape like what outline_profile from sil_tools.py expects — a boolean/thresholded 2-D array (see candidates.py line 34: np.asarray(Image.open(...)) > 127). experiments/silhouette-match/train.py: - Head.logits(self, f) (lines 35-38): `python def logits(self, f): x = torch.tensor(((np.atleast_2d(f) - self.mu) / self.sd).astype(np.float32)) with torch.no_grad(): return self.net(x).numpy()[0] if x.shape[0] == 1 else self.net(x).numpy() ` It accepts either a single 1-D feature vector or a 2-D batch (np.atleast_2d handles both), and returns a 1-D array of per-silhouette logits when given a single vector (squeezes batch dim via [0]). - load_head(path) (lines 66-71): `python def load_head(path): z = np.load(path, allow_pickle=True) net = make_net(len(z["mu"]), len(IDS), int(z["hidden"])) net.load_state_dict({k[2:]: torch.tensor(z[k]) for k in z.files if k.startswith("w_")}) net.eval() return Head(net, z["mu"], z["sd"]) ` Loads the .npz (e.g. head_v1.npz), rebuilds the net via make_net(d, n, hidden) (lines 41-42, a Linear → GELU → Dropout(0.3) → Linear MLP), and restores weights keyed w_* (stripping the w_ prefix to match state_dict() keys), plus mu/sd for the feature normalization done inside Head.logits. - IDS = [e["id"] for e in LIB] and SLOT = np.array([e["slot"] for e in LIB]) (lines 27-28) come from src/lib/styling/silhouettes.json — logits(f) returns one score per entry in that list, in that same order; to restrict to a garment's slot you index with np.nonzero(SLOT == slot)[0] the same way candidates.py line 45 does (head.logits(f)[idx]). A minimal match_one.py reusing this code correctly would therefore need to: build the mask for the one image, call Extractor().features([img], [mask])[0] to get the 542-d row, call load_head(path).logits(row) to get per-silhouette logits aligned to IDS/SLOT from src/lib/styling/silhouettes.json, then filter/sort by the garment's slot exactly as candidates.py` lines 42-49 do.

Found it. In src/components/garment-splitter.tsx line 90, the photo <img> uses w-full object-contain with a max-h-[60vh] cap. That combination forces the image into a box whose aspect ratio doesn't match the photo's own aspect ratio whenever the height cap kicks in (any portrait photo taller than ~60% of viewport width) — so object-contain letterboxes it, leaving blank margins. But the detection boxes are positioned as percentages of the wrapping frame, not the actual visible image content, so boxes land in the letterbox margin instead of on the garment. Since detection runs on original image pixels regardless of aspect ratio, uploading a batch of mixed portrait/landscape photos makes each review screen misalign differently — which reads as "messy overlap" as you flip through them. The fix is to stop forcing a mismatched box and let the image size itself naturally within the height cap, so the wrapping frame's bounds always exactly equal the visible image (no letterboxing, no coordinate drift):

Back to only the 2 pre-existing unrelated warnings, and all 251 tests pass. The dev server should hot-reload this change automatically. Found and fixed: src/components/garment-splitter.tsx line 90-92. The review photo's <img> had w-full object-contain combined with max-h-[60vh] — forcing it into a box whose aspect ratio often didn't match the photo's own ratio (any portrait photo, which is most phone photos). object-contain then letterboxed it, leaving blank margins. But the detection boxes are positioned as percentages of the wrapping frame, not the actual visible image — so boxes landed in the blank margin, misaligned by a different amount for every photo depending on its aspect ratio. Flipping through a batch of mixed-orientation uploads, each misaligned differently, is exactly the "messy overlap" you saw. Fixed by dropping w-full/object-contain so the image sizes itself naturally (max-w-full, height auto, capped at max-h-[60vh]) — the frame always exactly matches the visible image now, so box percentages line up regardless of orientation, and the queue (one GarmentSplitter dialog at a time, confirmed correct in uploader.tsx) was never actually the problem. Try uploading a batch again — the dev server should hot-reload this. Let me know if the boxes land correctly now.

Update(DECISIONS.md)
⎿  Added 18 lines
    239  - **Caught porting the model:** PyTorch `Linear` stores weight
          as `[out, in]`, so the naive `W[i][j]` affine (right for a `[
         in, out]` matrix, as in `colourPair.ts`'s already-transposed e
         xport) silently produced garbage here; fixed to `W[j][i]`. Als
         o the tower's Sequential has `Dropout` at index 0, so the expo
         rted keys are `t.1.*` / `t.3.*`, not `t.0.*` / `t.2.*`. Verifi
         ed by recomputing the same pairs in numpy straight from the ex
         ported JSON (bypassing PyTorch) and matching the TypeScript ou
         tput exactly before trusting the golden fixture.
    240  - **Wired into `pairScore.ts`:** `proportion` blends the old h
         and rule (`proportionScore`, fit/length only) with the model's
          score (`silhouetteModelScore`, using `bridgeSilhouette` match
         es) by `STYLING_CONFIG.silhouetteModel.weight` (default 1 = mo
         del only, matching the colour model's convention). `SILHOUETTE
         _PAIR_MODEL_ID` (ratings on 3 fixed pairs) is in the item fing
         erprint, so a retrained model re-scores stored pairs.
    241  - **Not done:** outerwear pairs still fall back to the hand ru
         le's `proportionScore` only, since outerwear bottoms don't exi
         st and the bridge only covers top/bottom. `silhouette_matches`

         p: no network, a fixed table scan over <=220 silhouettes).
    242 +                                                              
    243 +## Garment -> silhouette matcher (4a) made live: a Python subp
        +rocess, backfilled onto the demo account (2026-10-25/26)      
    244 +- **Why:** 4a was trained (see above) but never called; `pairS
        +core` only ever saw the attribute bridge. The user asked to cl
        +ose that gap and see it working on the demo account.          
    245 +- **How** (`experiments/silhouette-match/match_one.py`, `src/l
        +ib/ai/silhouetteMatch.ts`): there is no CLIP implementation an
        +ywhere in this app (checked: no transformers.js/onnx, no prior
        + child_process precedent in `src/`), and no deployment config 
        +(no vercel.json/Dockerfile) suggesting a serverless target tha
        +t would rule out shelling out to Python. Given tagging already
        + waits seconds on a vision API call, a few more seconds for a 
        +Python subprocess (reusing the exact trained `head_v1.npz` and
        + `features.py`, no reimplementation risk) was judged simpler a
        +nd safer than adding a JS ML stack. The tag route calls it fro
        +m its existing `after()` background callback, only for top/bot
        +tom/outerwear items with a cutout, and writes `items.silhouett
        +e_matches` (new nullable jsonb column, migration `202601010000
        +10`) only when the matcher returns something; failures leave i
        +t null so a later retry can still succeed.                    
    246 +- **Preprocessing:** the live cut-out (`@imgly/background-remo
        +val`, transparent PNG) is composited onto white and masked fro
        +m alpha >= 128, matching how the training images were prepared
        + (confirmed via `colour-extract.ts`'s own alpha-based mask con
        +vention).                                                     
    247 +- **pairScore.ts:** an explicitly empty match array (`[]`, mea
        +ning the matcher ran but found nothing confident) now falls ba
        +ck to the bridge too, not just `null`/`undefined` — otherwise 
        +a legitimate "no match" result would permanently disable the m
        +odel for that item instead of degrading to the heuristic.     
    248 +- **Backfilled** the demo account's 5 pre-existing tagged item
        +s (`scripts/backfill-silhouette-matches.mjs`, re-runnable, onl
        +y touches items where `silhouette_matches` is still null). Con
        +fidence scores came back low (0.10-0.28, vs 0.93 on a syntheti
        +c same-drawing sanity check) and one top-1 looked questionable
        + (wide-leg palazzo pants -> a skirt silhouette, with the corre
        +ct pants silhouette ranked second). Given only 5 real samples 
        +and no ground truth for them, this is not enough to say the li
        +ve accuracy falls short of the 80.9%/95.5% cross-validated num
        +bers — flagged to the user rather than asserted either way; a 
        +visual comparison page was generated locally (git-ignored, emb
        +eds real photos, never committed) so the user could judge by e
        +ye.                                                           
    249 +                                                              
    250 +## Upload review: box/frame misalignment, then overlap + hard-
        +to-toggle (2026-10-26)                                        
    251 +- **Why:** uploading several photos in one batch showed boxes 
        +misaligned on the photo, and after that was fixed, overlapping
        + transparent boxes were still hard to read and hard to tap the
        + right one.                                                   
    252 +- **Misalignment** (`src/components/garment-splitter.tsx`): th
        +e photo `<img>` used `w-full object-contain` under a `max-h-[6
        +0vh]` cap. Whenever the cap applied (any portrait photo, i.e. 
        +most phone photos), the img's CSS box no longer matched its ow
        +n aspect ratio, so `object-contain` letterboxed it — but the d
        +etection boxes are positioned as percentages of the *wrapping 
        +frame*, not the letterboxed content area, so they landed in th
        +e blank margin. Fixed by dropping `w-full`/`object-contain`: t
        +he image now sizes itself naturally (`max-w-full`, `height: au
        +to`, capped at `max-h-[60vh]`), so the frame's bounds always e
        +xactly equal the visible image for any aspect ratio.          
    253 +- **Overlap + toggle**: each detected box was a full-rectangle
        + button with a semi-transparent fill; overlapping detections (
        +common — garments are often adjacent or touching) stacked thei
        +r fills into a muddy blob and competed for taps (whichever box
        + was on top in DOM order won, not necessarily the one the user
        + meant). Fixed by making the box itself an outline only, `poin
        +ter-events-none` (overlapping outlines stay legible as crossin
        +g lines, never steal a tap), and moving the actual toggle to a
        + small fixed-size badge anchored at the box's corner (a checkm
        +ark/cross + number, solid background, always a consistent easy
        + tap target regardless of box size or overlap).               
    254 +- Not covered by the existing test suite (no jsdom/testing-lib
        +rary setup in this project; vitest here only exercises `src/li
        +b` pure functions) — verified by reasoning through the CSS box
        + model and by the user re-testing in the running dev server, n
        +ot by an automated test.                                      
    255 +                                                              
    256 +## Dark garments were invisible in the closet (2026-10-26)    
    257 +- **Why:** a cut-out's background is transparent; `.lightbox`'
        +s own background is a dark gradient (`#2b2b35` to `#15151c`). 
        +A black, navy or charcoal garment has almost no contrast again
        +st that and effectively disappears.                           
    258 +- **How** (`src/lib/styling/thumbBackdrop.ts`): a pure functio
        +n reusing `colourPair.ts`'s existing Lab conversion — below La
        +b lightness 32 (both thresholds picked by eye, not derived fro
        +m data), swap the thumbnail's backdrop to a warm neutral `#ded
        +7c7` (evoking cloth/linen, not a stark white that would clash

        +b_backdrop`, needs the `colors` column already on `items`) int
        +o `Rail` (`RailItem.backdrop`, an inline style override) and t
        +he closet's own 2-column grid view.

        +.ts`), which does not carry colour data yet — extending there

        + here.

         st that and effectively disappears.

         m data), swap the thumbnail's backdrop to a warm neutral `#ded
         7c7` (evoking cloth/linen, not a stark white that would clash

         b_backdrop`, needs the `colors` column already on `items`) int

Searched for 1 pattern, ran 1 shell command
The Fashion Aina pitch page is built in product-pitch/. Everything it needs is inside the folder (2.8 MB, no outside links), so you can copy it straight into your GitHub Pages repo. Open product-pitch/index.html to preview it locally. I named the folder product-pitch rather than "product pitch", because a space in a web address tends to break. The page runs in this order: - Hero: a playground photo, then the garments found in it, then their matched silhouettes, with the headline numbers. - Flow graph: all 7 stages, colour-coded. Tapping a stage jumps to its section. - Find and Describe: pick any of the 9 playground photos and click a box or garment. You see the crop, the background-removed cut-out, every tag, and the colours the picker measured. - Colour: the colour model's predicted ratings for 10 wardrobe colours as a heat grid, examples of what you rated, and why the small network on perceptual colour won. - Shape: the full 220-drawing library with family filters, and what the model actually reads off a silhouette (its outline widths and a grid of where its lines are). - Match examples: 12 garments matched to silhouettes, plus the accuracy chart going from 62% to 95.5%. - Silhouette-pair model: what you rated, its accuracy, and its favourite and least-favourite pairings. - Scoring: the weights, the rules that can veto a pair, and how pairs go from rule score to vision ranker to the top 5. - Design decisions and the tech stack. The 12 match examples come from a copy of the matcher retrained without those garments, so none of them were seen in training. 10 of 12 have one of your labelled silhouettes in the top 3; the 2 misses are shown with the reason. As you chose, the page includes the playground photos and the library drawings. Both come from third-party sources and are now headed for a public site. Your personal closet photos and the shop photos are left out. This is recorded in DECISIONS.md. I checked it in headless Chrome at desktop and phone width. All the clicks and hovers work, there are no errors, and nothing spills off the side on a phone. If you change data, re-run experiments/pitch/build.py to refresh the page's images and numbers. Searched for 1 pattern, ran 1 shell command
Here's where things stand: the UI work is done, the cut-out research is still running in the background, and phase 2 isn't finished yet. UI (committed as 7fb4710) - Themes: four of them. Atelier, a warm ivory/ink/terracotta light theme, is the new default. Noir is the previous dark look with lit light boxes, plus Rosé and Sage. You switch on the new "You" page, and the choice is remembered. - Default changed from dark to light: you'd earlier asked for a dark wardrobe, but black and navy garments vanished on it. Noir is one tap away if you prefer it. - New screens: - Today: an outfit of the day picked for the weather, your week, unworn pieces you could "rediscover", and stats. - Mix & match: swipe tops and bottoms and see the match score update live, with shuffle, lock and "best partner". - Saved looks and "Wore it" buttons, with a wear diary. - You: your colour palette, outfits per occasion with the missing piece named, and the theme picker. - Redesigned screens: - Closet: a colour filter and a rails/grid toggle. - Item page: colours, formality and warmth meters, "Mix with this", "Wore it". - Add and review: tap scales and chips instead of number boxes. - Desktop: a sidebar layout instead of a narrow phone column. - Weather: your OpenWeather key in .env.local is blank, so I used Open-Meteo, which needs no key. - Checks: typecheck, lint (no errors) and the production build pass. All 280 tests pass on their own runs. One existing test, in detections.test.ts, timed out in the full-suite run while the background agent was loading the machine; it passes alone, and I'll re-run the full suite when it's done. I also clicked through save → Saved page → "Wore it" → diary in a real browser, then removed the test rows from the demo account. Pipeline: one confirmed bug so far Several cut-outs in your closet are completely transparent. The background remover erased the whole garment and the app stored the empty result without checking. That's why the navy top, the black tank and the floral dress show as blank cards. The new light theme makes this visible; the dark theme hid it. How the chain works: 1. A Gemini call finds a box around each garment. 2. That region is cropped out of the full-size photo. 3. A general background remover (@imgly) runs on the crop. It doesn't know about clothing, so it keeps skin and bodies, and it can erase garments that are close in colour to the background. 4. Colours and the silhouette match are both measured from that cut-out, so a bad cut-out corrupts both. The tagger sees the original crop, so it isn't affected. The background agent is now testing other cut-out methods against hand-checked masks: a clothing-specific segmenter, box-prompted SAM-style models, and a human-parsing model to strip skin and hair. It's also looking at a quality gate for empty cut-outs and at why some crops are tiny (143×96 px). When it reports back, I'll check its evidence, wire the winning method into the app, and re-run the pipeline end to end.

     1 +/**                                                            
     2 + * Is a cut-out plausible? The same gate as experiments/cutout-
       +lab/cutout_one.py: the solid garment must cover between        
     3 + * 6% and 98.5% of the crop, and at most 35% of what is kept ma
       +y be half-transparent. Live failures it catches: fully         
     4 + * erased cut-outs (0% solid; 4 of the demo account's 23) and "
       +ghost" cut-outs where most of the garment came out             
     5 + * see-through (9 more). Pure; `rgba` is canvas ImageData pixel
       +s (4 bytes per pixel, alpha last).                             
     6 + */                                                            
     7 +export const CUTOUT_GATE = { minOpaque: 0.06, maxOpaque: 0.985,
       + maxSoftRatio: 0.35 } as const;                                
     8 +                                                               
     9 +export function cutoutGate(rgba: ArrayLike<number>): { ok: bool
       +ean; opaque: number; soft: number } {                          
    10 +  const n = Math.floor(rgba.length / 4);                       
    11 +  if (!n) return { ok: false, opaque: 0, soft: 0 };            
    12 +  let solid = 0;                                               
    13 +  let soft = 0;                                                
    14 +  for (let i = 3; i < rgba.length; i += 4) {                   
    15 +    const a = rgba[i] / 255;                                   
    16 +    if (a >= 0.5) solid++;                                     
    17 +    if (a > 0.1 && a < 0.9) soft++;                            
    18 +  }                                                            
    19 +  const opaque = solid / n;                                    
    20 +  const softShare = soft / n;                                  
    21 +  const ok =                                                   
    22 +    opaque >= CUTOUT_GATE.minOpaque &&                         
    23 +    opaque <= CUTOUT_GATE.maxOpaque &&                         
    24 +    softShare / Math.max(opaque + softShare, 1e-6) <= CUTOUT_GA
       +TE.maxSoftRatio;                                               
    25 +  return { ok, opaque, soft: softShare };                      
    26 +}

Tracing the full chain, I found the main issue: the tagger mislabeled the "Black Coat" box as checked trousers since its crop is mostly trousers, creating a duplicate and losing the coat. The cheap fix is to pass the detector's original "Black Coat" label as a hint instead of discarding it—checking the tagger and its prompt now.

Both parts are done, tested and committed: the UI redesign (7fb4710) and the pipeline fix (82df120). The cut-out was the main thing hurting results, and it's fixed with measured evidence. A few weaker stages further down the chain are still open; they're listed at the end. 1. UI redesign - Four themes: Atelier (warm ivory, ink and terracotta) is the new default. Noir is your earlier dark look with lit light boxes, plus Rosé and Sage. You switch on the new "You" page and the choice is remembered. - Default changed from dark to light: you'd asked for a dark wardrobe, but black and navy clothes vanished on it. Noir is one tap away if you prefer it. - New screens: - Today: an outfit of the day that suits the weather and skips anything you wore in the last few days. Plus your week, unworn pieces to "rediscover", and stats. - Mix & match: swipe tops and bottoms and see the match score live, with shuffle, lock and "best partner". - Saved looks and "Wore it", with a wear diary. - You: your colour palette, outfits per occasion (it names the missing piece, e.g. "add a bottom for formal"), and the theme picker. - Redesigned: - Closet: a colour filter and a rails/grid toggle. - Item page: colours, formality and warmth, "Mix with this". - Add flow: drag-and-drop. - Review screen: tap scales and chips instead of number boxes. - Desktop: a sidebar layout instead of a narrow phone column. - Inspiration: Whering's outfit shuffle, Acloset and Alta's weather-based daily outfit, Indyx's wardrobe stats. - Weather: your OpenWeather key in .env.local is blank, so I used Open-Meteo, which needs no key. 2. Pipeline: what was wrong and what I changed - The cut-out (mask) was broken: 13 of your 23 garment cut-outs were completely transparent or see-through, and the app saved them without checking. That's why several garments showed as blank cards. - Testing: a background agent compared 7 methods against 24 masks it drew and checked by eye. A clothing-parser model scored 0.90 overlap with the true mask versus 0.56 for the old method. Colour accuracy measured from the cut-outs went from 0.47 to 0.89. - New server cut-out: the server now re-cuts every newly tagged item with the clothing parser. It saves the result next to the old file instead of overwriting it, re-measures colours, and re-runs the silhouette match. It's a local Python step like your silhouette matcher, so a serverless deploy won't have it. - Safer browser cut-out: for that case it pads the image before cutting (overlap 0.56 → 0.75) and rejects empty or see-through results instead of storing them. - Existing items: I re-cut all 24 demo items and re-scored pairs. Every garment now shows. I saved a backup of the old values first, in a git-ignored file. - Tagger fix from a real photo test: I uploaded a coat/shirt/check-trousers photo through the app. The open coat got tagged as the trousers underneath it. The garment detector had already labelled that box "Black Coat", so the tagger now receives that label as a hint (tagger.v13). Correct slots went from 13/15 to 15/15 on your hand-labelled crops, with no regressions. - Cleanup: deleting an item now removes all its files, including old cut-outs. The test uploads, saved looks and wear entries are removed, so the demo account is back to its earlier contents, apart from the re-cut items and re-scored pairs above. Checks: typecheck, lint and the production build pass, and all 288 tests pass. Still weak, in order 1. Colour names: a black coat comes out "charcoal", a white shirt "pale grey", brown/cream gingham "charcoal". This feeds pair scoring directly. Fixing it properly needs a small hand-labelled colour set, which doesn't exist yet. 2. Silhouette matcher: low confidence and some wrong picks (khaki trousers → "classic shorts"), even with clean cut-outs. 3. Intermittent "Not signed in" on upload: it happened in 1 of 3 test runs and didn't come back on retry. I haven't found the cause. Colour naming is the next thing I'd tackle. All of this is recorded in STATUS.md and DECISIONS.md. Claude's response
Let me first understand exactly how colours are picked and named today.
Listed 1 directory, ran 1 shell command
I found the root cause: colors get matched to the nearest of 121 paint chips using average Lab values, but photographed black, white, and fine patterns shift enough (lighting, resizing) to snap to the wrong chip. Before fixing this, I'll check whether the datasets already contain any human-labeled colors to use as ground truth.

I'll set up a new experiments/colour-naming/ folder combining the 24 demo garments and 15 test crops, then hand-label acceptable colour names for each to score the picker against. First, let me check how the Python original and TypeScript tests are set up.

Found the bug: the "transition colours" step meant to remove blurry boundaries was wrongly classifying smooth gradients (like shaded denim) as transitions, deleting two-thirds of the jeans' color clusters and leaving only shadow and highlight. I'm now checking whether this same issue explains the other misses.
Ran 1 shell command
Three issues explain most misses: averaging washes out lit vs. shadow tones, paint-chip names don't match camera-recorded black/white ranges, and low-res resizing blurs fine patterns like gingham. I'll test fixes one at a time—naming by lit-tone percentile, calibrating swatches to camera range, tightening the edge-detection rule, and raising sampling resolution—starting by making resize resolution a backward-compatible parameter.

Running a grid search across 576 settings for the 37 garments, using leave-one-out so each garment is scored on settings tuned from the other 36 to avoid overfitting the test set.
Ran 1 shell command
The search is bigger than I estimated (1,200 combinations) and is still running in the background. While it runs, one consideration about the calibration idea. It risks overcorrecting real mid-tones, for example turning a genuine charcoal garment into black. The labelled set has no true charcoal or light-grey garment except the grey ribbed trousers. So whatever wins, I'll also check it against the existing picker unit tests, which include greys and stripes, before porting.

Combining all four fixes raises accuracy to 32/37 primary and 1/3 two-colour, with patterns remaining the main weakness. Let me look at what's still being missed.
Ran 1 shell command
The remaining misses split into borderline color calls, a badly underexposed photo, and gingham patterns losing their light squares — that last one's a clear bug, so I'll trace it next.
Ran 1 shell command
Found it: the lighting step merges light clusters into the main color as highlights, but on patterned garments that wrongly swallows gingham/print whites. The fix is to check the garment's pattern field (already determined before color measurement) and preserve distinct light clusters as a second color when patterned—so next I'll pull the pattern info for each test garment.

What you'll see: - Live now: the redesigned UI and the fixed cut-outs. All 24 demo garments were re-cut, so none are blank any more. - Not live yet: the colour fix is still experimental. Colour names in the app are the old ones, so a black coat still says "charcoal". I'm finishing that now. - Adding photos works end to end, but the server cut-out step runs on this Mac, so keep it awake. Packaging it as a deployable app (Docker) The reason Docker is needed: two pipeline steps, the silhouette matcher and the new cut-out, are Python models that the Next.js server calls directly. That rules out Vercel-style serverless hosting. You need a long-running container on a VM or a container host. The database, login and file storage are already on hosted Supabase, so they move as they are. Step: Docker image What's involved: Node + Python in one image, CPU-only PyTorch, model weights (~650 MB) downloaded at build time so the first request isn't slow. Image ≈ 3 GB. Effort: ~½ day ──────────────────────────────────────── Step: Keep models loaded What's involved: Right now each cut-out reloads its model (~8 s per garment). A small always-on Python worker cuts that to ~1 s. Not required, but strongly recommended. Effort: ~½ day ──────────────────────────────────────── Step: Host + domain What's involved: A machine with ≥ 4 GB RAM (a small VPS from Hetzner or DigitalOcean, or Fly.io / Railway / Render, roughly $10–30/month), HTTPS, environment secrets, and adding the new domain to Supabase's allowed login URLs. Effort: ~½ day ──────────────────────────────────────── Step: Must-fix before strangers use it What's involved: The intermittent "Not signed in" upload error, a health check, error logging. Effort: ~½–1 day ──────────────────────────────────────── Step: Spec's full launch list (M8) What's involved: Rate limits, Sentry, installable phone app, privacy pages, staging + production copies. Effort: +2–3 days My estimate: about 1.5–2 days to a working deployed app you can share, and 4–5 days to the spec's full production standard. Mostly that's careful setup rather than new features. One decision would change the plan. If you'd rather avoid running a server, the Python steps can be dropped in production. The app already falls back to the browser cut-out, which is now padded and quality-gated, and to the simpler silhouette rules. Then it could deploy to Vercel in a few hours, at the cost of lower-quality cut-outs (0.75 overlap vs 0.90). I'll finish the colour work first. It's waiting on one validation run. After that, let me know whether you want the Docker deployment and where you'd like to host it.

The colour fix is done, committed (3e3ac8d), and live on http://localhost:3000. The demo closet's colours have been re-measured. Results I had no ground truth, so I built a labelled set first: 39 garments, with the acceptable colour names marked by eye. Two were excluded because their masks are wrong, leaving 37 scored.
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬───────┐ │ │ Before │ After │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Main colour right │ 20/37 │ 32/37 │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Two-colour fabrics (gingham, block print): both colours │ 0/3 │ 3/3 │ │ found │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴───────┘
To guard against tuning to the test set, I tuned on half the garments and scored on the other half, both ways round: 10/13 vs 4/13 for the old picker, and 22/24 vs 14/24. Both halves independently chose the same settings, and those are what shipped. Honest caveat: on brand-new photos expect somewhat less than 32/37. What was wrong, and the fixes 1. A real bug: the picker deleted most of some garments. A step meant to drop the blurry edge between two colours also removed the middle of any fabric under natural shading. The jeans lost two-thirds of their pixels and came out "61% black". 2. Colours were named by their average, shadows included. A cream satin skirt averaged out to "taupe". The picker now names each colour by its well-lit part. 3. The reference colours were paint chips. Cameras rarely record pure white, so white tops came out "pale grey". Names are now matched against the colour list as a camera records it. 4. Light pattern colours were treated as highlights. The gingham's white squares disappeared into the blue. When the tagger says a garment is patterned, a clearly lighter colour is now kept as part of the pattern. What you'll see in the app - White tops now say white instead of pale grey, and the cream skirt says beige instead of taupe. - The light-blue top is now powder blue + white, the gingham light wash + white, and the floral set gets its pinks + white. - Pairs are being re-scored in the background with the new colours. - The 4 items whose tags you had already confirmed were left untouched. The old colours are backed up in a git-ignored file. Still wrong - Black wool coat → "charcoal". The other three black garments are right. - A badly underexposed rust dress → "oxblood". - Jeans read as plain grey. That's true to those pixels, but you'd call it "mid wash". All of this is recorded in DECISIONS.md and STATUS.md. Typecheck, lint, all 291 tests and the production build pass. Ready for the Docker deployment whenever you are. If we use a docker and all will I get a link I can share with other people ?
Claude's response
Yes. Strictly, Docker only packages the app; the shareable link comes from running that package on a hosting service. With Fly.io you'd get a permanent HTTPS address like https://closet-aina.fly.dev, and anyone can open it on their phone or laptop. You can put it on your own domain later if you want. What happens when someone opens the link - They sign in with their email and get a magic link, or tap the demo button. - Everyone who uses their own email gets a private closet. - Everyone who uses the demo button shares one closet, so they'd see and change each other's clothes. That's fine for a quick look, less so for real use. Three things to fix before sharing widely 1. Sign-in emails. Supabase's built-in email sender only allows a few emails per hour, so if several people sign up at once, some won't get their link. The fix is to connect a free email service such as Resend (~15 minutes; you'd create the account). 2. AI costs. Every upload calls Gemini to detect, tag and pair garments. You already have a daily spend cap and a demo-account limit configured, so costs can't run away, but busy days may hit the cap and pause tagging. 3. The intermittent "Not signed in" upload error I saw once. I should fix that before strangers see it. If you want to show someone today, before any of that: I can open a temporary public link straight to this Mac using a tunnel (Cloudflare or ngrok). That takes about 5 minutes, but it only works while your Mac is on and awake, and it's slower. It's fine for showing a few friends tonight, not as a permanent link. Since that puts your local app on the public internet, I'll only do it if you say so. So the options are: - Temporary link now (tunnel, about 5 minutes, needs your Mac on), or - Permanent link (Docker + Fly.io, same day: about 3–5 hours of my work, plus a few minutes of you creating the Fly account and logging in). Which do you want? Or both: the tunnel now, then the permanent deploy.

     1 +/**

       +t.hf.space). Behind a hosting proxy the request URL the        
     3 + * server sees is the internal one (http://0.0.0.0:3000), so re
       +directs built from it would send the visitor nowhere;          
     4 + * the proxy's x-forwarded-host / x-forwarded-proto headers car
       +ry the public one. Header values are checked to be a           
     5 + * plain host[:port] and http/https, so a malformed header fall
       +s back to the request URL. Pure.                               
     6 + */                                                            
     7 +export function publicOrigin(request: { url: string; headers: H
       +eaders }): string {                                            
     8 +  const fallback = new URL(request.url);                       
     9 +  const host = request.headers.get("x-forwarded-host")?.split("
       +,")[0].trim();                                                 
    10 +  if (!host || !/^[a-z0-9.-]+(:\d{1,5})?$/i.test(host)) return 
       +fallback.origin;                                               
    11 +  const proto = request.headers.get("x-forwarded-proto")?.split
       +(",")[0].trim();                                               
    12 +  const scheme = proto === "http" || proto === "https" ? proto 
       +: fallback.protocol.replace(":", "");                          
    13 +  return `${scheme}://${host}`;                                
    14 +}

Notably, the attribute bridge (which ignores the image entirely) crushes the shipped trained matcher (0.63 vs 0.19 top-1), and with the gate it hits 0.66/0.88 with zero family errors — meaning the live matcher was actually hurting results. Since it draws on different evidence, I'll export its scores and test fusing it with image + text.

Fusing in the bridge gives mixed results (top-1 and MRR improve, but top-5 slips slightly), and on only 32 garments that's not a clear win—so I'll ship image + text + family gate, keeping the gated bridge as fallback. Next, I'll check whether this holds up separately on the demo closet and test-set photo halves.

        +-validated") had only ever been tested on its own             
    419 +  training domain: shop photos and whole-photo cut-outs from a
        + different segmenter. The app feeds it tight box crops        
    420 +  cut by the clothes parser. A new live-domain test set (`expe
        +riments/silhouette-eval/labels.json`: 32 tops and             
    421 +  bottoms from the demo closet and datasets/tagger-test, the a
        +pp's actual cut-outs, acceptable silhouettes picked by        
    422 +  name and by eye, Claude, not independent) showed: top-1 0.19
        +, top-5 0.50, and 10 of 18 trousers put in the skirt          
    423 +  or shorts family. It was worse than the attribute-only bridg
        +e it replaced (0.63 / 0.88).                                  
    424 +- **Results (`eval.py`; top-1 / top-5 / MRR / bottoms in the w
        +rong family):**

    427 +  - CLIP zero-shot vs the mean render of each silhouette 0.28

    434 +- **Bias check:** labels were picked partly by name and text m

    435 +  A visual sheet (`sheet.py` -> `sheet.png`: garment, old top-

That doesn't help. Even at the 30th percentile the black coat reads lightness ~14, which still sits nearer charcoal than black once the camera range is applied, and one other garment got worse. The camera genuinely recorded that wool as very dark grey, and telling black from charcoal would need an exposure reference in the photo. I'll record it as a negative result and leave the shipped picker alone. Here's where the model-quality work stands. The cut-out agent is still running. Done and committed (ac32e99) 1. Silhouette matching: replaced. This was the biggest gain. The old matcher had only ever been tested on its own training photos. On the app's real cut-outs it put 10 of 18 trousers in the skirt or shorts family, and it was worse than the simple fallback it replaced. The new matcher compares the garment's image with both the silhouette drawings and their names, and only considers the family the tagger's category allows.
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬───────┐ │ On 32 labelled garments from your closet │ Before │ After │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Right silhouette ranked first │ 0.19 │ 0.72 │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Right silhouette in the top 5 │ 0.50 │ 0.94 │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Trousers matched as skirts or shorts │ 10/18 │ 0/18 │ └──────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴───────┘
- Honesty checks: the gain holds on both halves of the set. I also checked the new picks against the actual drawings by eye, because my labels partly use names and so does the new method; the visual check confirms them. - Confidence now means something: it was 0.1–0.4 before. Now, when it says ~0.7, it's right about 70% of the time. - Your closet is updated: khaki trousers are now matched as dhoti pants (was classic shorts), and the palazzo as palazzo pants (was paper-bag shorts). 2. Ranking bug fixed. "Ranking is not a permutation" made the app throw away good AI rankings; it happened 12 times in one log. Malformed answers are now repaired, and good passes are kept. 3. Colour: the black-coat fix didn't work (above), so nothing changed there. Still running: the cut-out agent, on skin patches, the white top worn on skin, the belt kept on the shirt, and rough edges on small crops. For you, tomorrow: press "Re-score all pairs" (Style page) once the demo AI budget resets. It's the only step that brings the new silhouette matches into the match scores. I held off today because, with no budget left, a re-score would replace your AI-ranked scores with rule-only ones. Can't be measured here: overall outfit match quality. Your rated outfits live in a labeler/data/ folder that isn't on this Mac. If you can copy it over, I can measure and tune matching against your own ratings.

The UI is far better, 1. why is the user asked to box the garments themselves? why not use the segmenter? the segmenter was working alright I belive? also in the mix and match I can see that many pairs have been left unscored why is that the case ?
Claude's response
Good questions. I'll check the facts before answering both.
Ran 1 shell command
Both have clear causes, and neither is the segmenter misbehaving. 1. Why you were asked to draw boxes Normally you aren't. Every photo first goes to an AI garment finder that boxes each garment automatically; you only untick what you don't want. In my earlier end-to-end test it found all 5 pieces (coat, shirt, trousers, bag, shoes) in about 6 seconds. What you hit today is the daily AI budget. The finder is a Gemini call, and the demo account's token budget is used up (the server log shows POST /api/items/detect 429). When the finder fails, the app falls back to "drag a box round each garment". That fallback is what you saw. You're right that the local clothes parser I use for cut-outs could do this job. It runs on this machine and costs nothing, and it already labels every pixel as top, trousers, skirt, dress, bag, shoes and so on. Boxes around those regions would make garment-finding work even with no AI budget, offline, or when Gemini is rate-limited. The AI finder is still probably better for flat-lays of several separate garments and for accessories. So my suggestion: use the parser as the automatic fallback (measured against the 9 hand-boxed test photos), and consider making it the primary finder if it scores close. 2. Why many Mix & match pairs are unscored Your closet has 11 tops × 11 bottoms = 121 possible pairs: - 83 are scored. Those are exactly the pairs that share an occasion (casual with casual, work with work…). - 38 are unscored. The app has a rule that two items are only scored together if they share an occasion, so a festive top is never paired with gym shorts. In Mix & match you're choosing pairs yourself, so that rule just leaves gaps. - Of the 83, only 16 have an AI-ranked score. The other 67 use the rule-based score, because the AI ranker ran out of budget, the same cause as #1. The fix: compute the rule-based score for every pair on the spot in Mix & match. It's local, instant and free. Cross-occasion pairs would show a note like "different occasions: work top with festive skirt". The AI ranker stays limited to sensible pairs to save budget. And tomorrow's "Re-score all pairs" will turn more of the 67 rule scores into AI-ranked ones. ⏺ User answered Claude's questions: ⎿  · Should I build these two fixes now? → As long as the segmenter is the gemini one when credits are there that is good enough. in that case ther is nothing to change right I believe ?
Right, nothing to change there. When there are credits, every photo goes to the Gemini garment finder and the boxes appear automatically. You only saw the manual boxes today because the budget had run out, and that resets tomorrow. Even then nothing breaks: you can draw boxes or add the whole photo. One thing worth knowing: the demo account shares a single daily budget among everyone who uses it, so if several people try the shared link on the same day, they can run it out again. If that happens, raising DEMO_DAILY_TOKENS in .env.local fixes it, at the cost of more Gemini spend. On the hosted version you'd change it in the Space's settings instead. I haven't changed Mix & match. The 38 unscored pairs are cross-occasion combinations, so they'll stay unscored until you want that changed. Instant rule-based scores for every pair would take me about 30 minutes whenever you want it.

     1 +"use client";                                                  
     2 +                                                               
     3 +/**                                                            
     4 + * The browser side of bring-your-own-key (src/lib/ai/byok.ts):
       + the user's Gemini key lives in this device's local            
     5 + * storage only and rides along, as `x-gemini-key`, on the requ
       +ests that call the AI. The downloadable apps add               
     6 + * "AinaApp" to their user agent and must have a key; the web s
       +ite works without one (on the owner's key and limits).         
     7 + */                                                            
     8 +const STORAGE = "aina-gemini-key";                             
     9 +export const GEMINI_KEY_PATTERN = /^AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}$/;   
    10 +export const KEY_CHANGED = "aina-key-changed";                 
    11 +                                                               
    12 +export const isApp = () => typeof navigator !== "undefined" && 
       +/\bAinaApp\b/.test(navigator.userAgent);                       
    13 +                                                               
    14 +export function getGeminiKey(): string | null {                
    15 +  if (typeof localStorage === "undefined") return null;        
    16 +  const k = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE);                     
    17 +  return k && GEMINI_KEY_PATTERN.test(k) ? k : null;           
    18 +}                                                              
    19 +                                                               
    20 +export function setGeminiKey(key: string | null) {             
    21 +  if (key) localStorage.setItem(STORAGE, key);                 
    22 +  else localStorage.removeItem(STORAGE);                       
    23 +  window.dispatchEvent(new Event(KEY_CHANGED));                
    24 +}                                                              
    25 +                                                               
    26 +/** Headers for a request that may call the AI: the user's own 
       +key when one is saved. */                                      
    27 +export function aiHeaders(): Record<string, string> {          
    28 +  const k = getGeminiKey();                                    
    29 +  return k ? { "x-gemini-key": k } : {};                       
    30 +}

     1 +// Builds the download page for GitHub Pages: release/index.htm

Done (tested, not committed yet) - Bring your own key: the apps now require the user's own Gemini key, and your Vercel site keeps using yours. - The key is stored only on the user's device and sent only with their own requests. The server never stores or logs it. - Calls made on a user's key don't count against your daily budget or spend cap. - The apps can never fall back to your key. - Tested: with no key the app is refused with a clear message; a fake key gets "Gemini refused your API key"; once a key is saved the prompt goes away. - Apps: the desktop app (Mac/Linux) and Android app no longer contain or need any settings file or keys. They open your Vercel site in an app window. - Download page: three download buttons, a short "get your free Gemini key" guide, and a "use it in your browser" link. Generated by node scripts/make-download-page.mjs <owner/repo> <site-url> into release/index.html plus the logo, ready for GitHub Pages. - .vercelignore: your .env.local and the datasets can never be uploaded to Vercel. I am deploying more than one app there is already another app on it what should I do about that ?
Claude's response
It depends on which "there" you mean, but none of them is a problem. GitHub Pages (your website): most likely what you mean. Don't put my index.html at the root of your site, or it will replace your existing homepage. Give Aina its own folder instead: your-site-repo/
├── index.html ← your existing site, untouched ├── (your other app's files) └── aina/ ├── index.html ← copy of release/index.html └── aina-logo.svg ← copy of release/aina-logo.svg
The page will then be at https://<your-site>/aina/. Nothing in it needs changing: the download buttons and the website link are full URLs, and the logo is loaded from the same folder. To show it from your main site, add a link to /aina/ wherever you list your projects. If your site is built with a framework (Jekyll, Astro, Next export…) rather than plain HTML files, put the aina folder wherever static files go: public/aina/ for Astro, Next or Vite; the repo root for Jekyll. Vercel: no conflict. Each Vercel project is separate, with its own address, settings and keys. Aina is project aina at aina-psi.vercel.app, and your other app keeps its own. One caution: the Hobby plan's free usage limits are shared across all your projects, but a personal demo won't come close. Supabase: if your other app uses the same Supabase project, Aina's tables (items, outfits, pair_scores, looks…) sit next to its tables. That's fine as long as the names don't collide, and since Aina is already working there, they don't. The real limit is the free plan: one project's storage (photos) and database size are shared by both apps. If you meant something else by "there", tell me which and I'll adjust.

Can I create a new supa base project ?
Claude's response
Yes, and keeping Aina in its own project is cleaner: separate data, storage and limits from your other app. On the free plan you can have 2 active projects. Free projects pause after about a week with no activity, and you can resume them from the dashboard. Nothing in Aina is tied to the current project. The database layout is all in supabase/migrations/ (10 files, including the photo storage bucket and its access rules), and there's a script that creates the demo account. Your part (about 5 minutes) 1. Go to supabase.com → New project. Name it, e.g. aina, and pick the region nearest your users. 2. Set a database password and keep it somewhere safe. I'll need you to type it once in step 4. 3.
